name: Adam Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most mornings I take the truck log, check the tools, and go where the fault board sends our line crew. I have a vocational certificate and apprenticeship behind me, but I still test every connection as if I were new. The work I like is restoring a street after wind has pulled a branch through the wires. I am less keen on a tablet asking me to tick boxes with cold fingers, and I have never used an AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I’d say a little faster paperwork is fine if the crew still checks the line itself. Our job is to restore power safely, and I do not want a screen substituting for a test meter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our mortgage is covered and my wife Lila and I have over six months saved, so the hype does not unsettle our budget. I would still be cross if managers used it as a reason to rush a repair sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the truck routine exactly as it is and ask the supervisor where any automatic form text comes from. In the first year I would compare a few completed forms with my handwritten notes before signing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. The children still need their lunches packed, whatever gets put in the office computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which form would you check first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fault report after a broken service wire. I would compare the address, the isolation time and the test result with the notes I made in the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put any of the family savings to work differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Lila and I keep that money for the mortgage or a bad stretch of callouts, not for a tool purchase.

say: **Faster forms** are acceptable when the field crew still verifies the repair.
A **test meter** matters more than a generated line of text.
think: Our **savings** and steady pay keep this from touching the household budget.
I would resist **rushed signoffs** even if the new forms look tidy.
do: **Keep** the current truck and line testing routine.
**Compare** each automatic fault report with handwritten truck notes and meter readings before signing it.
feel: **Calm**, because work and family finances stay broadly steady.
S0.quote: Our job is to restore power safely, and I do not want a screen substituting for a test meter.
fieldNote: His **familiar routine** is a point of pride rather than a refusal to check evidence.
The **mortgage buffer** means a minor software change has little effect on household security.

steps.text: Keep existing truck checks and line testing routine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the office not to make a repair slot shorter because a program drew a neat route. The call desk can change fast, but a line still takes the time it takes to isolate and test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think some dispatch and buying posts will shrink before our field crew does. If managers then push those office savings into tight repair targets, my overtime could become less reliable, and our mortgage is sized for my current earnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep working the current rota and write down each job where travel or isolation takes longer than the new estimate. During the first year I’d take that log to my supervisor and ask for the time standard to be corrected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit stubborn about it. I would rather argue over a job sheet than let a shorter target become normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as proof that the target is too short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three fault jobs with the route, isolation and testing times written beside the estimate. The supervisor can dispute my numbers, but then we can look at the same sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If overtime fell, what would go first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would trim weekend trips before touching the children’s school activities. Lila’s pay helps, but I do not want the mortgage covered by savings every month.

say: **Repair slots** cannot be shortened simply because the route plan is faster.
**Field testing** remains necessary while office work changes.
think: Reduced **office posts** might lead to tighter targets and weaker overtime.
The **mortgage** relies on current earnings more than I like to admit.
do: **Log** travel and isolation times against automated job estimates.
**Take** three examples to the supervisor and seek a corrected time standard.
**Trim** weekend trips if overtime actually falls.
feel: **Uneasy** about overtime, with a stubborn wish to prove the numbers.
S1.quote: I would rather argue over a job sheet than let a shorter target become normal.
fieldNote: He sees **office change** as a route to pressure on his own hours and pay.
His **job log** is concrete evidence for a one-to-one discussion with the supervisor, not group action.

steps.text: Keep current line repair rota and record each job time
Cut weekend trips if linework overtime actually falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the thinking AI in 2028 could take the fault desk and plans, but the robots that can work on the lines come about 2031. Until then the company needs people who can climb, test and make a safe repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is not a lot for a forty-three-year-old with two school-age children and a mortgage. There are other line jobs nearby, but if every company buys the same robots around 2031, a move across town may buy only a little time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask payroll for a plain account of my base pay without callouts and check our mortgage against that figure. If robots start taking our jobs after 2031, I would apply for a field maintenance opening at a nearby utility before paying for any course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, though I would keep going to work. I can make a plan on paper, but I cannot make another company promise me a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children at the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say I still have work now and that we might skip a holiday while I check the numbers. I would not tell them I had lost a job before any letter arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the nearby maintenance post asks for a new qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask whether the employer pays for it and whether an opening actually exists. I would not spend our mortgage cushion on a course advertised as a maybe.

say: **Thinking AI** can change fault planning in 2028 before field robots arrive around 2031.
**Line crews** remain needed through the physical work gap.
think: A nearby **line job** may offer only short relief if other utilities adopt robots too.
My **mortgage** makes three years feel shorter than it sounds.
do: **Check** base pay without callouts against the mortgage payment.
**Skip** a holiday if repair income falls.
**Apply** for nearby field maintenance work after 2031 if robots reduce repair shifts.
feel: **Anxious**, but still making a cautious plan.
S2.quote: I can make a plan on paper, but I cannot make another company promise me a place.
fieldNote: He keeps the **2028 and 2031** stages separate in his account of risk.
He would ask about **funded qualifications** before spending savings, and no training commitment has been made.

steps.text: Skip a family holiday if line repair income falls
Apply for nearby utility maintenance if robots reduce repair shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my mates five years is enough for the company to show us a proper training plan, if one is coming. The hands-on robots would arrive around 2034; no one should pretend a planning program in 2031 can already repair a cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not like studying off a screen and I have never opened an AI assistant. Still, I could learn a specific testing procedure if someone demonstrates it on real equipment and there is paid time; my certificate came from doing as well as reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the training manager for a demonstration day on the network testing gear and for the pay rate of any new post. In the first year after 2031, if the company offers paid training and a real vacancy, I’d enrol; otherwise I’d keep my field shifts and monitor openings nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but less pressed than in the fast version. Five years gives me time to see a working machine before betting the household on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the demonstration useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let me handle the tester and compare its reading with a known fault, not just watch slides. A network testing post has to make sense on a wet afternoon, not just on a training slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Lila favour the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Lila would ask first about the wage and the hours around school pickup. I expect she would support it if those numbers held up.

say: **Five years** lets the employer show real training and pay terms.
**2031 planning AI** is different from a field robot expected around 2034.
think: I could learn **testing gear** through a physical demonstration and paid practice.
The **family budget** cannot rest on a course without a real vacancy.
do: **Request** a hands-on testing demonstration and the new post’s pay rate.
**Enrol** after 2031 only if paid training and an actual opening are offered.
feel: **Worried**, but able to inspect the option before committing.
S3.quote: A network testing post has to make sense on a wet afternoon, not just on a training slide.
fieldNote: His **resistance** is specific to untried software, not an inability to learn practical equipment.
His **conditional enrolment** depends on paid time, a genuine vacancy and workable family hours.

steps.text: Keep field shifts while checking testing role pay and duties
Enrol in paid network testing training after 2031 if an opening exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade gives us time to finish our mortgage plans and teach the next crews properly. Thinking AI in 2036 may change the office, while robots around 2039 might change the field work I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three I could still have years of earning ahead, and the children may need help starting out. I do not want to call it retirement just because a robot turns up; I need to know what the mortgage balance and my actual options are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my present line crew job and review the mortgage and savings with Lila each birthday. In the first year after 2036 I’d ask for the exact pay and duties of any inspection post; if it offers enough to cover our bills, I’d apply before field robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious, but able to breathe. Ten years lets me count real bills instead of guessing at a future cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection job pays less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare the shortfall against our fixed bills and the children’s likely costs. If it meant drawing down savings every month, I would stay on field work while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI system yourself by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the inspection role requires it and someone teaches me on the equipment I will use. A sales demonstration would not persuade me to change jobs.

say: **Ten years** allows careful mortgage and work planning.
**2036 office AI** and field robots around 2039 affect different parts of linework.
think: I may still need **earnings** after fifty-three to help the children start out.
I will not call a **robot arrival** retirement without checking the money.
do: **Review** mortgage and savings with Lila each birthday.
**Apply** for an inspection post after 2036 only if pay covers fixed household bills.
feel: **Cautious**, with room to count bills and options.
S4.quote: I do not want to call it retirement just because a robot turns up; I need to know what the mortgage balance and my actual options are.
fieldNote: His **annual review** keeps family costs and remaining debt visible through the long runway.
He sets a **pay threshold** for an inspection move rather than promising to accept any offer.

steps.text: Keep line crew job while reviewing mortgage and savings annually
Apply for inspection after 2036 only if pay covers fixed bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because it leaves very little time between the office changing and field robots coming. A written account of available posts, their pay and any funded training would help me plan without risking the mortgage money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I wish you had asked what happens to a crew when one person no longer trusts the work order. On a line, stopping together matters more than winning an argument afterward.

portrait: **Adam Santos**, 43, is an experienced electricity lineworker with a vocational certificate and apprenticeship.
He and wife Lila have **two children**, a mortgage, higher pay and over six months of savings.
He has **never used AI**, prefers known tools and checks line repairs with a test meter and handwritten notes.
In **Steady Disruption**, his concern shifts from office automation to shorter repair targets and weaker overtime.
He fears **AGI by 2028** most, while a longer runway lets him inspect training and job terms before changing roles.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives him little time to find secure work before capable field robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **post and pay terms** would let him judge a possible move without spending the mortgage cushion.
A real **funded training** offer would matter more than a general promise about future jobs.
headlineQuote: On a line, stopping together matters more than winning an argument afterward.
